title: Back to the source
hookLine: picture nine: the river flows, the flowers are red (Ox-Herding 9)
tomorrow: stay on the quiet mountain, or walk into the market?

cards: Come home from a long trip and your own street looks strange for a day, then just right. Here's the puzzle in Kuoan's ninth picture. After the empty circle, you'd expect light, or nothing at all.
Instead: a riverbank, a tree, flowers. And the verse scolds itself: too many steps taken to come back to the root and the source. Better to have been blind and deaf from the start.
Why go back to plain things after the circle?

teach.b: The answer is in the preface. From the beginning, it says, all was pure, without a speck of dust. The herder watches things grow and fade from a place of stillness.
The waters are blue, the mountains green. He sits alone and watches them change.
The verse ends: inside his hut he isn't looking for anything outside; the river flows on by itself, the flowers are red by themselves.
Kuoan sounds almost sheepish: all that searching, catching, taming and riding, to arrive at what was there before the first step. That's the Zen teaching of return.
Awakening doesn't trade this world for a better one; it hands this one back, as it is. A Chinese teacher, Qingyuan Weixin, put it in a saying recorded in Zen collections.
Before he practiced, mountains were mountains and rivers were rivers. Then, with some insight, mountains were no longer mountains, and rivers no longer rivers.
Now, at rest, mountains are just mountains again, and rivers again rivers.
So the puzzle solves itself. The empty circle wasn't the end, because emptiness was never somewhere else.
The river was flowing the whole time. Only the one looking changed.

how: Zen teachers point to plain things, mountains, rivers, flowers, as the place awakening is lived. People on this path look at ordinary things as they are.

games.q: what does “back to the source” mean?
o: a monk's return to the temple where he trained
the ninth picture: the plain world, seen as it is
a pilgrimage to the spring where a river begins

games.q: back to the source: tap the pairs.
p: the river flows, the flowers are red

s: Kuoan's verse for picture nine praises all the steps it took to get there
it scolds them: too many steps; better to have been blind and deaf from the start.
Qingyuan's saying ends with mountains being mountains again
first mountains, then not mountains, then just mountains, seen as they are.
awakening in Zen means escaping to a better world
the popular version. picture nine hands this world back, as it is.

games.q: a friend back from a year of travel says home feels dull now, and she needs the next big trip to feel awake. what would picture nine say?
o: the river flows here too; awake means seeing home as it is.
she's right: awakening lives in new places, so keep moving.
awake means the world should feel strange to her forever.
games.why: after the empty circle, Kuoan draws a riverbank and red flowers. Qingyuan's mountains become mountains again: the same world, seen plainly.

practice: Look at some water, a glass of it will do, or a plant or a flower if one's near. For the two minutes, see it as just what it is, before any thought about it: water, wet; a leaf, green.

wordCard.voice: Back to the source: Kuoan's ninth picture. After emptiness, the world returns as it is: the river flows, the flowers are red.

orig.note: Chinese: returning to the root, back to the source; the title of Kuoan's ninth picture.

carryVoice: The line to keep: the river flows, and it was flowing all along. Nine of ten.

sources.ref: Kuoan Shiyuan, Ten Ox-Herding Pictures, picture 9 'Returning to the Origin, Back to the Source' (preface and verse)
Qingyuan Weixin's saying on mountains and rivers (Wudeng Huiyuan, Compendium of the Five Lamps)
